pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 3: Information Security

Our exam results, bank balances, health records and photos are stored as data. In this unit you will learn the three key principles that keep information secure, the laws that protect people’s creative work, and how investigators track down those who break information-security laws.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.3.3.1** Recognise data threats and means of protection.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.3.3.1.1** Discuss the key principles of information security (confidentiality, integrity and availability).
- **B7.3.3.1.2** Explore the legal issues regarding intellectual property rights (copyright, patent, trademark, piracy, copyright infringement).
- **B7.3.3.1.3** Evaluate information security forensic auditing and criminal laws against offenders.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 9.1 The Key Principles of Information Security
- 9.2 Intellectual Property Rights and the Law
- 9.3 Forensic Auditing and Criminal Laws Against Offenders

**Core competencies developed:** Digital Literacy (DL5.1, DL6.5, DL6.6), Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1, CC8.4, CC9.5).

lessons.title: The Key Principles of Information Security

pages.title: The Key Principles of Information Security
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain confidentiality, integrity and availability;
- apply the principles to real-life scenarios.
**Information security** is the protection of information and information systems from unauthorised access, use, change, disruption or destruction. It is built on three key principles known as the **CIA triad**.
[[fig:c7-f19|Figure 18: The CIA triad]]
| **Principle** | **Meaning** | **Example** | **How it is protected** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Only **authorised** people can see or use the information | Only you and your parents should see your report card online; only you should know your Mobile Money PIN | Passwords and PINs, user accounts and permissions, encryption, locking screens |
| Integrity | Information is **accurate, complete and not changed** without permission | A learner must not be able to change exam scores in the school database | Permissions (read-only), backups, checksums, audit logs, digital signatures |
| Availability | Information and systems are **accessible when needed** by authorised users | WAEC results portal must work on results day; a hospital must access patient records in an emergency | Backups, power backup (UPS, generators), antivirus, maintenance, extra servers |

pages.title: The Key Principles of Information Security (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity — Scenario analysis (pairs)**
Decide which principle (C, I or A) is broken in each scenario: (1) A hacker changes the price of goods on an online shop. (2) A friend reads your WhatsApp chats while you are away. (3) The school server crashes on the day reports are due, and there is no backup. (4) A bank worker shares customers’ account balances. (5) A virus encrypts all files on a computer and demands payment. (Answers: 1 – I, 2 – C, 3 – A, 4 – C, 5 – A and I.)

lessons.title: Intellectual Property Rights and the Law

pages.title: Intellectual Property Rights and the Law
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain copyright, patent and trademark;
- explain piracy and copyright infringement;
- distinguish between freeware, shareware and crippleware;
- discuss consequences of breaking intellectual property laws.
**Intellectual property (IP)** refers to creations of the mind: inventions, books, music, films, software, designs, brand names and logos. **Intellectual property rights** are legal rights that give creators control over the use of their creations and allow them to benefit from their work.
| **Right** | **Protects** | **Example** | **Ghanaian law** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Copyright © | Original creative works: books, music, films, software, photos, artwork, websites. Protection is automatic once the work is created; no registration is required (though registration helps as proof). | A Ghanaian musician’s song; the code of a mobile app; this textbook | Copyright Act, 2005 (Act 690); administered by the **Copyright Office** |
| Patent | New, useful inventions (products or processes). The inventor must apply, and if the patent is granted, gets exclusive rights for a fixed period (usually 20 years). | A new design of solar-powered water pump | Patents Act, 2003 (Act 657); Registrar-General’s Department |
| Trademark ™ / ® | Names, logos, slogans and symbols that identify a company’s goods or services. ® means registered. | The MTN, Vodafone/Telecel or Kalyppo logos | Trade-Marks Act, 2004 (Act 664) |

pages.title: Piracy and copyright infringement
pages.body:
## Piracy and copyright infringement
- **Copyright infringement** is using copyrighted work without permission, for example copying, distributing, performing or adapting it.
- **Software piracy** is the unauthorised copying, installation, sharing or selling of software, such as installing one licensed copy on many computers, using “cracked” software or key generators, or selling pirated CDs.
- **Media piracy** includes illegal downloading or sharing of films, music and e-books, and selling pirated DVDs.
- **Plagiarism** is presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own without acknowledging them. It is an academic offence even when it is not a crime.
## Software licensing: freeware, shareware and crippleware
| **Type** | **Meaning** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Freeware | Software that is free to use without time limit, but the author keeps the copyright; you may not usually modify or sell it. | Google Chrome, Zoom (basic plan), Adobe Acrobat Reader, VLC∗ |
| Shareware | Software you can try free for a limited time (trial). You must pay to keep using it after the trial. | WinRAR (trial), many games and utilities |
| Crippleware | A version of software with important features disabled (e.g. cannot save or print, or adds a watermark) until you pay for the full version. | A video editor that adds a watermark until you buy it |
| Open-source software | The source code is freely available; anyone may use, study, change and share it under its licence. | LibreOffice, Firefox, Linux, VLC∗, Python |
| Proprietary (commercial) software | Must be bought or subscribed to; the licence sets strict rules on how many devices may use it. | Microsoft 365, Adobe Photoshop |

pages.title: Piracy and copyright infringement (continued)
pages.body:
∗VLC is both free of charge and open-source.
## Consequences of breaking intellectual property laws
- **Criminal penalties:** fines, imprisonment, or both, under Ghana’s Copyright Act and related laws.
- **Civil action:** the owner can sue for damages (compensation) and court orders to stop the infringement.
- **Confiscation** of pirated goods and equipment used to make them.
- **Security risks:** pirated software often contains viruses and malware, and does not receive security updates.
- **Loss to creators and the economy:** artists and software developers lose income, and the government loses tax revenue.
- **School sanctions** for plagiarism.
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection** Ghanaian creative artists, through bodies such as the **Ghana Music Rights Organisation (GHAMRO)**, collect royalties when their songs are broadcast or performed. Buying original music, films and software supports Ghanaian creators.
> 🧪 **Activity — Discussion**
In groups, discuss: Is it wrong to download a film from an illegal website if you cannot afford to pay for it? Differentiate between copyright, patent and trademark issues in your answer, and suggest legal alternatives (e.g. free, licensed streaming services, public libraries, open educational resources).

lessons.title: Forensic Auditing and Criminal Laws Against Offenders

pages.title: Forensic Auditing and Criminal Laws Against Offenders
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain how offenders of data security breaches are identified;
- discuss the laws protecting data and sanctions for breaching them;
- identify common data security breaches people overlook.
## Information security forensic auditing
**Digital (computer) forensics** is the scientific collection, preservation and analysis of electronic evidence so that it can be used in court. A **security audit** is a systematic check of an organisation’s systems, records and logs to see whether security rules are being followed and to detect breaches. Together, **forensic auditing** helps investigators answer: What happened? When? How? Who did it?
**How offenders are identified**
1. **Detection and reporting:** a victim reports the incident, or security software raises an alert.
2. **Securing the evidence:** investigators make exact copies (“forensic images”) of hard drives and phones so the originals are not changed, and record a **chain of custody** (who handled the evidence and when).
3. **Analysing logs and metadata:** system logs show who logged in, at what time, from which **IP address** and device; file metadata shows when files were created or changed.
4. **Tracing transactions:** Mobile Money and bank transfers, phone numbers (registered with Ghana Card) and email headers are traced.
5. **Recovering deleted data** and examining messages, browsing history and social media accounts.
6. **CCTV and witness evidence** may link a person to a device or location.
7. **Reporting:** findings are written up and presented to the police, the prosecutor and the court.

pages.title: Ghanaian laws that protect data
pages.body:
## Ghanaian laws that protect data
| **Law** | **What it does** |
|---|---|
| Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038) | Established the **Cyber Security Authority (CSA)**; protects critical information infrastructure; criminalises online child sexual abuse material, sexual extortion, non-consensual sharing of intimate images and other cybercrimes. Some offences carry prison sentences of up to 25 years. |
| Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772) | Makes electronic records and signatures legal, and criminalises hacking (unauthorised access), interception of data, computer fraud and damaging computer systems. |
| Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) | Protects personal data; requires organisations that collect personal data to register with the **Data Protection Commission** and to keep data secure, accurate and used only for stated purposes. |
| Copyright Act, 2005 (Act 690) | Protects creative works including software; penalises piracy. |
| Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29) | Covers general crimes such as fraud by false pretences (e.g. sakawa scams), which apply when committed online. |

pages.title: Common breaches that people overlook
pages.body:
## Common breaches that people overlook
| **Common breach** | **Why it matters** | **Possible consequence** |
|---|---|---|
| Sharing your password or Mobile Money PIN with friends | Anyone with your PIN can steal your money or impersonate you | Financial loss; you may be held responsible for actions done with your account |
| Using a friend’s phone or account without permission | Unauthorised access | An offence under the Electronic Transactions Act |
| Forwarding someone’s private photos or chats | Breach of privacy | Serious offences under the Cybersecurity Act; school discipline |
| Installing pirated or “cracked” software | Copyright infringement; malware | Fines; loss of data |
| Posting other people’s personal information (phone numbers, addresses) | Breach of data protection | Civil or criminal action |
| Leaving a computer logged in and unattended | Others can access your accounts | Data theft or misuse |
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection — Report cybercrime** The **Cyber Security Authority** runs a 24-hour Cybersecurity/Cybercrime Incident Reporting Point of Contact: **call or text 292**, **WhatsApp 0501603111**, or email **report@csa.gov.gh**. You can also report to the **Cybercrime Unit of the Ghana Police Service**.
> 🧪 **Activity**
Watch a video of how offenders of data security breaches are identified. Then, in groups, list three common data security breaches in your community and the sanctions that could apply. Make sure every group member contributes.
